title: Real joy
hookLine: real joy is a serious thing, deeper than cheerfulness (Letters 23)

cards: Scroll any feed for a minute and count the smiles. Beaches, birthday cakes, a dog in sunglasses. Everyone is having a wonderful time, all the time.
And yet it's possible to close the app feeling a little flatter than when it opened. Seneca never saw a feed, but he knew the gap between looking happy and being glad.
In the twenty-third letter he gives Lucilius one instruction above all the others, two words in Latin. An odd kind of order, because it commands something that seems to just happen to us.

teach.b: Disce gaudere. Learn how to feel joy. Seneca says to do this before anything else, which tells you he thought joy was a skill, not luck.

teach.h: REAL JOY IS A SERIOUS THING.
teach.b: Then a surprising claim: real joy is a serious thing. Not grim. Weighty, like the difference between a sparkler and a hearth.
Laughter, he says, isn't proof of joy. The mind has to be lifted, confident, steady, above everything that comes and goes. Cheerfulness can be loud and gone in an hour.
Joy, in his sense, sits low and stays. Where does it come from? Pleasures from outside, he says, sit on the surface.
The joy he wants for Lucilius springs from inside, from the best part of a person: a good conscience, honest intentions, right actions, a mind that doesn't depend on applause.
Picture a mine: what lies on the surface yields little, and the rich ore runs in a deep vein. If your gladness depends on the weather, the inbox, or someone's mood, it's on loan.

teach.h: NOTHING OUTSIDE CAN TAKE IT BACK.
teach.b: If it comes from the kind of person you're becoming, nothing outside can repossess it. The Stoic word for good feelings came up on day two hundred eighty-seven. Here Seneca adds that you can practice it.
You learn joy the way you learn a language: badly at first, then a little better.

how: Some readers of Seneca keep a short evening note of one quiet joy that came from their own conduct rather than from luck or praise.

o: a steady gladness that springs from inside
the burst of fun you get at a great party
being cheerful and smiling all day long

s: Seneca says laughter proves you're joyful
he says laughter isn't proof; the mind must be lifted and steady.
Seneca treats joy as something you can learn
his first instruction to Lucilius is disce gaudere: learn joy.
for Seneca, real joy means being grim
serious means weighty and lasting, not gloomy.

games.q: your friend got great news and posted fifty smiling photos. a week later they seem empty. what would Seneca point to?
o: outside pleasures run shallow; joy that lasts springs from inside.
joy is impossible, so don't bother.
games.why: Seneca says joy that comes from outside stays on the surface; the lasting kind comes from the best part of a person.

practice: Let your shoulders drop and look for one quiet joy that needs no applause: something you did well that nobody saw, a kindness you're glad you gave, the plain fact of being warm and breathing. Don't make it bigger than it is.
Let it sit low, like a coal rather than a firework.

wordCard.voice: Real joy. Seneca's gaudium: a serious, steady gladness that springs from inside, deeper than cheerfulness, and something you can learn. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: joy. Seneca uses it for the steady gladness of a good mind, as against passing pleasure (voluptas).

carryVoice: Your line: learn how to feel joy. A hearth, not a sparkler. That's day four hundred fifty-three.
